source: Dounas-Frazer, Van De Bogart, Stetzer, Lewandowski (2016) Investigating the role of model-based reasoning while troubleshooting an electric circuit
finding: Eight student pairs repaired a faulty two-stage op-amp circuit. Five used the split-half strategy. Using it did not make repair faster or slower.
numbers: N=8 pairs from 2 institutions (CU, UM). Pairs D to H used split-half, in the second half of the session. Pairs A and E repaired about twice as fast as the rest; only E used split-half.
quote: Pairs who used the Split-Half Strategy did not repair the circuit significantly faster or slower than those who did not.
limits: No statistics, no control of fault or order. Small N, think-aloud, physics students, one circuit with the fault in stage 2 so a midpoint test was easy. Authors say they did not compare groups.
agent_relevance: Do not assume half-split alone gives speed. Other factors (early model, luck, which part is replaced first) can dominate. Measure total test count, not strategy label.

source: Dounas-Frazer, Van De Bogart, Stetzer, Lewandowski (2016) Investigating the role of model-based reasoning while troubleshooting an electric circuit
finding: All five split-half pairs first built a two-subsystem model with a gain per stage, predicted stage outputs, then compared predictions to measurements.
numbers: 5 of 5 split-half pairs showed model construction, prediction and comparison.
limits: Qualitative coding by the authors. Cannot tell if the model caused the split or just co-occurred.
agent_relevance: Half-split needs a model that says what each half should output. The agent should write down expected values per block before it picks the split point.

source: Dounas-Frazer, Van De Bogart, Stetzer, Lewandowski (2016) Investigating the role of model-based reasoning while troubleshooting an electric circuit
finding: Most pairs swapped parts early and made extra unneeded changes. All pairs replaced the 100 ohm resistor; all but one replaced the faulty op-amp.
numbers: 8 of 8 pairs replaced the resistor, 7 of 8 the op-amp; resistor replaced before op-amp in every case; many extra revisions.
limits: Same small sample. The resistor value was a planted fault, so replacement was correct.
agent_relevance: Parts swapping before isolation is common human behaviour. Count unneeded edits as a cost in our own agent tests.

source: Dounas-Frazer, Stetzer, Lewandowski (2016) Electronics lab instructors' approaches to troubleshooting instruction
finding: Instructors named two common search strategies: forward topographic (measure from input toward output) and split-half (binary search at midpoint). About half stressed treating a circuit as testable subsystems.
numbers: 20 interviews, 18 institutions. About half of instructors stressed subsystem decomposition. Almost all called troubleshooting important; only half said they directly assess it.
quote: The split-half strategy ... is a way to iteratively reduce the problem space through a binary search
limits: Self-report from instructors, not student performance. Selected from the authors' network. No efficiency data.
agent_relevance: Experts' stated strategy list is short (forward trace, binary split). Both are cheap to encode as operators; teaching practice gives no proof they work.

source: Kim, Park, Yun, Lee (2026) Why Do AI Agents Systematically Fail at Cloud Root Cause Analysis?
finding: A baseline multi-agent RCA system on OpenRCA found the full root cause (component, time, reason) rarely. Accuracy was low in every model.
numbers: 335 incidents, 5 models, 1,675 runs, mean 11.1 steps per run, 609.9 hours, about 1.38 billion tokens. Perfect accuracy 3.9% (Claude Sonnet 4) to 12.5% (Gemini 2.5 Pro). Earlier Claude Sonnet 3.5 result 11.3%.
limits: One framework (Controller-Executor with Python kernel). Telemetry-heavy task with logs and metrics, not part-swapping troubleshooting.
agent_relevance: Fault isolation in noisy real data is far from solved. A search scaffold must be tested on tasks where the truth is hard to see.

source: Kim, Park, Yun, Lee (2026) Why Do AI Agents Systematically Fail at Cloud Root Cause Analysis?
finding: Dominant failures were shared by all models. Wrong reading of data and narrowed exploration were most common. Treating a symptom as the cause and no cross-check also occurred.
numbers: Hallucination in interpretation 71.2% of runs; incomplete exploration 63.9%; symptom-as-cause 39.9%; code error 27.2% (1.8% Gemini to 65.5% Claude Sonnet 4); no cross-validation 18.6%. Categories overlap.
limits: Labels assigned by the authors' process; percentages sum above 100.
agent_relevance: These are the search-strategy failures our schema must block: premature stop at a symptom, one hypothesis, one data source. Code can force a second source and a coverage list.

source: Kim, Park, Yun, Lee (2026) Why Do AI Agents Systematically Fail at Cloud Root Cause Analysis?
finding: Prompt-only fixes did not help. A hypothesis template widened exploration but the model still misread data. Warning text about pitfalls was echoed but not obeyed.
numbers: 70 Bank tasks, Claude Sonnet 4. Neither hypothesis-driven nor pitfall-aware prompting gave a meaningful gain in root-cause identification.
limits: Single model and single domain for this test. No effect sizes given.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence against solving search errors by instruction alone. Move the check into code, not into the prompt.

source: Kim, Park, Yun, Lee (2026) Why Do AI Agents Systematically Fail at Cloud Root Cause Analysis?
finding: A structural change (show the Controller the generated code and raw errors) cut inter-agent failures and steps.
numbers: Pitfall rate down about 14 (GPT-5 mini) and 15 (Claude Sonnet 4) percentage points. Steps per run 11.9 to 9.2 (-22.1%). Time -22.3%. Tokens per step +24.8% (68K to 85K); total tokens -1.6%. Perfect detections in Bank: GPT-5 mini 0 to 2 (0.0% to 4.9%), Gemini 2.5 Pro 1 to 3, Solar Pro 2 2 to 3.
limits: Gains in accuracy are 1 to 2 cases out of about 41 per model. Not significant on their own.
agent_relevance: Efficiency gains (fewer steps) are firmer than accuracy gains. Passing raw tool output between roles is cheap and helps.

source: Wang, Yu et al. (2026) Cloud-OpsBench: A Reproducible Benchmark for Agentic Root Cause Analysis in Cloud Systems
finding: Right final answer often came without a closed chain of evidence. Process scores lag outcome scores a lot.
numbers: 452 fault cases, 40 root cause types, 10 models, 20-step cap, temperature 0. GPT-5 joint accuracy 0.68 on both systems but evidence closure 0.21 (OnlineBoutique) and 0.15 (TrainTicket). DeepSeek-V4-Flash best, JRA 0.76, ECR 0.38.
limits: Replay of recorded snapshots, not live systems. Process metrics depend on the authors' evidence graph.
agent_relevance: Score our agent on evidence closure and steps, not only on the final answer. Correct-by-luck diagnosis hides bad search.

source: Wang, Yu et al. (2026) Cloud-OpsBench: A Reproducible Benchmark for Agentic Root Cause Analysis in Cloud Systems
finding: Longer runs were not better. Strong models used 5 to 7 steps. The weakest used 14 to 16 steps with many repeated calls and low accuracy.
numbers: OnlineBoutique steps: GPT-5 5.56, Qwen3.5-Plus 5.92, Qwen3-14B 14.58, Qwen3-8B 16.01. Repeated-action rate 0.46 and 0.28 for the two small models vs about 0.00 for strong ones. Evidence efficiency 0.64 (GPT-5) vs 0.37 (Qwen3-8B). JRA 0.19 for Qwen3-8B.
limits: Models differ in size and family at once, so steps and capability are confounded.
agent_relevance: A repeat-action detector (RAR) is a cheap, code-side guard for the loop. Step count alone is not a quality signal.

source: Wang, Yu et al. (2026) Cloud-OpsBench: A Reproducible Benchmark for Agentic Root Cause Analysis in Cloud Systems
finding: Reusing past experience helped on one system, not clearly on the other, and did not improve evidence closure.
numbers: 3 models. OnlineBoutique JRA 0.70 base, 0.79 with 3 retrieved trajectories (ICL), 0.76 with runbook-style SOP; ECR 0.39 to 0.59 and 0.61. TrainTicket JRA 0.58 base, 0.56 ICL, 0.62 SOP; ECR 0.18, 0.18, 0.17.
limits: Retrieval by symptom, not by cause; same symptom maps to several causes, which the authors give as the reason for weak transfer.
agent_relevance: Case library memory helps only if keyed well. Abstracted runbooks (SOP) transferred more steadily than raw cases.

source: Wang, Yu et al. (2026) Cloud-OpsBench: A Reproducible Benchmark for Agentic Root Cause Analysis in Cloud Systems
finding: Qualitative failure modes of search control: commit after one abnormal pod, no redirect when a path weakens, and keep querying after decisive evidence.
numbers: Purposive sample of JRA=0 trajectories from 10 models; no prevalence estimate given.
quote: These trajectories reflect weak control over hypothesis revision, diagnostic branching, and stopping.
limits: Authors state the sample does not estimate prevalence.
agent_relevance: Three code-checkable rules: do not stop on first abnormal; force a branch change after a refuted path; stop when decisive evidence appears.

source: Chen, Shetty et al. (2025) AIOpsLab: A Holistic Framework to Evaluate AI Agents for Enabling Autonomous Clouds
finding: Agents did well on detection, much worse on localization and root cause. Cheaper or faster agents were less accurate.
numbers: 48-problem suite. Table 4 (13 localization and 22 RCA problems): GPT-4-with-shell RCA 40.90% in 4.81 steps; ReAct RCA 45.45%; FLASH RCA 36.36%; GPT-3.5 RCA 9.09% in 14.00 steps. Localization top-1: GPT-4 61.54%, ReAct 53.85%, FLASH 46.15%, GPT-3.5 30.77%.
limits: Very small per-cell N (13 to 22 problems). Single run per agent.
agent_relevance: Baseline numbers for LLM fault isolation; a weak model took 3 times as many steps for a fraction of the accuracy.

source: Chen, Shetty et al. (2025) AIOpsLab: A Holistic Framework to Evaluate AI Agents for Enabling Autonomous Clouds
finding: Step budget helps some agents and not others. Gains plateau fast for weak agents.
numbers: FLASH peaked at 59.32% overall accuracy at a 20-step limit. For GPT-3.5, more than 5 steps only raised token cost.
quote: increasing the step limit beyond 5 does not yield better performance but merely increases the token consumption
limits: One step-limit sweep, small problem set.
agent_relevance: Adaptive stopping should depend on the model: cap steps early for weak backbones.

source: Bertolazzi, Mazzaccara, Merlo, Bernardi (2023) ChatGPT's Information Seeking Strategy: Insights from the 20-Questions Game
finding: ChatGPT asked far more questions than an optimal half-splitting questioner and rarely halved the space after the first turn.
numbers: 8-candidate games. Optimal 3.5 questions, simple baseline 4.0, ChatGPT 7.24 (Wilcoxon p<0.001). Constraint-seeking (halving) questions: optimal 57.14%, ChatGPT 73.77%. It kept asking after only one candidate remained in 56.67% of games (29.29% of questions unnecessary). 39.44% of second-turn questions had zero information gain.
quote: On average N/2 turns without the half-split, log2 N + 1/2 with it.
limits: One closed model (ChatGPT 3.5), hierarchical hypothesis spaces from feature norms. Questioner, answerer and oracle were all ChatGPT.
agent_relevance: Model-chosen splits are unreliable and the model loses track of what is eliminated. Code should keep the candidate list.

source: Bertolazzi, Mazzaccara, Merlo, Bernardi (2023) ChatGPT's Information Seeking Strategy: Insights from the 20-Questions Game
finding: Telling the model to list the updated candidate set each turn moved it toward the optimal agent. Space size and feature source mattered little.
numbers: Stepwise prompt: 6.4 vs 7.24 questions; contradictory questions 13.50 to 8.42; spoiled games (kept asking after target revealed) 12.22 to 7.78. 8 to 16 candidates: optimal +1 question, ChatGPT +1.43.
quote: Our conjecture is reinforced by the increased performance reached by the model when prompted to explicitly update the space
limits: Explicit listing helped but did not remove failure: it still missed when the target was revealed.
agent_relevance: Support for a code-side hypothesis ledger: the weakness is bookkeeping, not world knowledge.

source: Do Reasoning Models Ask Better Questions? (2026) arXiv 2601.17716
finding: Chain-of-thought reasoning raised information gain per turn and cut turns, mainly when the task was only partly observable.
numbers: Guess My City, 40 cities, 30-turn cap, 120 games per model, max 5.32 bits. Qwen3-8B partly observable: win rate 0.08 to 0.94 with reasoning, turns 29.60 to 15.82. Qwen3-30B Instruct 0.10 vs Thinking 0.93 (turns 29.13 vs 14.88). Fully observable: Qwen3-8B turns 16.02 to 8.86; Thinking-30B 7.12 turns, 0.78 bits per turn.
quote: Larger models exhibit higher assertiveness in selecting optimal queries
limits: Read from the arXiv HTML page. Text and Table 2 disagree on some figures. Oracle and pruner are small models. 40 cities, geography only.
agent_relevance: Reasoning mode matters most when the situation is unclear. Use it at the test-selection step, not everywhere.

source: Do Reasoning Models Ask Better Questions? (2026) arXiv 2601.17716
finding: Models picked the max-information question in only a minority of turns even though they were told to halve the options.
numbers: Optimal candidate chosen in 19 to 36% of turns (Qwen3-8B 0.36 fully observable, 0.19 partly; Qwen3-30B Thinking 0.26 and 0.25). Qwen3-8B considered 9.74 candidates per turn vs 7.63 in partial observability but chose the best less often.
limits: Page prompt says to eliminate about half; the paper does not frame the result as a halving failure.
agent_relevance: Let the model generate several candidate tests; let code score them by expected split and pick.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: Uncertainty-Aware Planning Enhances Information Seeking in LLMs
finding: An explicit expected-information-gain planner raised success in 20 questions, medical diagnosis and a troubleshooting dialogue set.
numbers: Average +38.1% success rate over direct prompting across 5 datasets and 5 LLMs (Llama3-70B +46.6%). Troubleshooting (FloDial, 153 faults, 20-turn cap) GPT-4 43.7% to 67.3%, fewest turns in successes 7.8. Llama3-70B closed-set: 28.8% to 47.1%, turns in successes 15.7 to 7.6. Beats CoT-SC by 33.8%, Reflexion by 29.9%, adapted ToT by 12.4%.
limits: Answerer is simulated by GPT-4 on simplified tasks; planning depth limited to three steps for cost; authors say benchmarks are simplified.
agent_relevance: Closest published test of EIG-driven question choice on a troubleshooting-like set; supports code scoring of tests.

source: Choudhury et al. (2025) BED-LLM: Intelligent Information Gathering with LLMs and Bayesian Experimental Design
finding: Full expected information gain beat both direct prompting and a split-the-candidates baseline in 20 Questions.
numbers: Animals, Celebrities, Things, 100 targets each. Mean +37.4 percentage points over prompt-only; success more than doubled in over half of setups and never fell. The split baseline equals maximum marginal entropy under deterministic answers.
quote: BED-LLM's final success rate is typically more than double that of Prompt-Only
limits: Authors' own baselines. Answerer is an LLM. The split baseline used the same filtering step, so it was strong.
agent_relevance: Pure balanced splitting is not the best rule when answers are noisy; use information gain, not entropy alone.

source: Choudhury et al. (2025) BED-LLM: Intelligent Information Gathering with LLMs and Bayesian Experimental Design
finding: Entropy-only scoring gives no gain when answers are noisy, because a split can be balanced yet uninformative.
numbers: The Entropy ablation gave no improvement over prompt-only in the preference-elicitation experiments (section 6.2). An example question has high marginal entropy and equally high conditional entropy, so little is learned.
limits: Preference elicitation, not fault finding. Ablation sizes in the appendix not examined.
agent_relevance: In faulty-instrument troubleshooting, tests with unreliable readings should be down-weighted, not just halved.

source: Feldman, Provan, van Gemund (2010) A Model-Based Active Testing Approach to Sequential Diagnosis (JAIR 39)
finding: A greedy test chooser (FractalG) cut the number of remaining diagnoses nearly as fast as exhaustive search and far faster in run time.
numbers: ISCAS85/74XXX circuits. Geometric decay of remaining minimal-cardinality diagnoses: mean rate p=0.7, mean R2=0.88. ATPG variant p=0.73, R2=0.84. Greedy vs exhaustive on 74182: decay rate gap 5.4%. Exhaustive timed out above 20 controls; greedy took 1 s to 40 min.
quote: This happens even with a coarse-grained device model
limits: Authors say optimality can be made arbitrarily bad by encoding truth tables. Gains assume independent controls. Circuits, one printer case study.
agent_relevance: Greedy test selection is a defensible default. Each good test cuts candidates by a constant factor, so stop rules can use the decay curve.

source: Pattipati, Patterson-Hine, Iverson et al. (1997) Multiple Fault Isolation in Redundant Systems (NASA-Ames final report)
finding: Optimal single-fault test sequencing with test costs is solved by dynamic programming or AND/OR graph search with entropy and Huffman-coding lower bounds. Multiple-fault isolation is super-exponential, so near-optimal methods are used.
numbers: Dynamic programming cost O(3^n) in tests. Near-optimal families: AOT, limited-search AO*, multi-step information heuristics, Lagrangian relaxation. The report cites TEAMS software. On Graham and Garey's pathological example, certainty-equivalence did better than information heuristics.
limits: Engineering report with synthetic and system examples; the figures I opened are not human data. Test models assume known costs and probabilities.
agent_relevance: Cost-weighted selection is a solved design pattern with a clear greedy form: gain per cost, with look-ahead only if budget allows. Greedy info rules have known bad cases.

source: Rouse (1978) Human Problem Solving Performance in a Fault Diagnosis Task, IEEE Trans. Syst. Man Cybern. 8
finding: In two experiments on graphically displayed networks, human diagnosis drifted from optimal as problem size grew. Forced pacing pushed people toward brute force. A computer aid for bookkeeping cut wrong diagnoses.
numbers: Factors: problem size, forced pacing, computer aiding, training. The NTRS page gives directions only, no numbers.
quote: Human performance deviates from optimality as problem size increases
limits: Only the abstract page was read, not the paper; no N or effect sizes available here.
agent_relevance: Time pressure should be treated as a risk for brute-force search. Offload bookkeeping to code.

source: Morris, Rouse (1985) Effects of type of knowledge upon human problem solving in a process control task
finding: Giving operators procedures, principles or both changed test scores but did not improve diagnosis of unfamiliar failures. Procedures did make control steadier.
numbers: 4 instruction groups in the PLANT simulation. Instructions improved written knowledge scores; no effect on production or on unfamiliar-failure diagnosis; procedures gave more stable control.
limits: Abstract only; no N or effect sizes on the page. Null result for principles, with reasons only speculated.
agent_relevance: Telling the agent how the system works may not help isolation of new faults. The test is whether the scaffold changes behaviour, not knowledge.

source: Starr, Storey (2026) Theory of Troubleshooting (arXiv 2602.10540)
finding: A grounded theory of developers' troubleshooting built around confusion. No test of search strategy such as half-split. Reports intuition leads and wrong jumps are common.
numbers: 27 interviews, 570 total years of experience; saturation after 12; 451 focus codes and 8 core categories. Cites 458 developers (91% did not use a debugger) and 89 debugging episodes at about 7 edit-run cycles per fix.
limits: Only the first 100,000 of about 210,000 characters were read. No half-split or cost content in that part. Interview data, no efficiency measure.
agent_relevance: Little direct support for structured search from software developers' accounts. Intuition-led poking is the human default.

source: Schaafstal, Schraagen, van Berlo (2000) Cognitive task analysis and innovation of training: the case of structured troubleshooting, Human Factors 42
finding: Technicians trained in a structured method (general strategy plus multi-level functional breakdown) solved about twice as many malfunctions in less time than the traditionally trained group.
numbers: Radar-system course; equal knowledge pretest scores; about double the malfunctions solved. Exact counts not seen.
limits: Search snippets only. Quasi-experiment with one course; no effect sizes read. Not opened.
agent_relevance: Best-known intervention result for functional decomposition plus a fixed strategy. Worth opening in full next.

source: Gugerty (2007) Cognitive components of troubleshooting strategies, Thinking and Reasoning 13
finding: Untrained students backtrack from wrong outputs. Learning the more efficient elimination strategy needed both domain knowledge and a general reductio-style rule.
numbers: 50 college students, simple digital networks. Both knowledge types were needed to raise elimination use significantly.
limits: Abstract snippets only. Not opened.
agent_relevance: Candidate elimination is not spontaneous. Give the agent the elimination rule explicitly, plus a domain model.

source: Besnard, Bastien-Toniazzo (1999) Expert error in trouble-shooting: an exploratory study in electronics, Int J Human-Computer Studies 50
finding: In a faulty circuit task novices did better than experts. Experts used symptom-fault rules and acted irrelevantly on atypical symptom patterns.
numbers: Numbers not seen.
limits: Abstract-level snippets only; small exploratory study. Not opened.
agent_relevance: Rival to the view that expertise equals better search: familiar-pattern shortcuts fail on atypical cases. Matches a risk in symptomatic search.

source: Rasmussen, Jensen (1974) Mental procedures in real-life tasks: a case study of electronic trouble-shooting, Ergonomics 17
finding: Original source of topographic search (follow the correct function) versus symptomatic search (match abnormal pattern). Secondary sources say symptomatic search suits familiar faults and topographic suits novel ones.
numbers: No numbers seen. Original paper was not retrievable.
limits: Only secondary summaries; searches returned no full text. URL is from memory and unverified.
agent_relevance: Map: symptomatic is a fast pattern match; topographic walks the structure. Agent should switch to topographic when pattern match gives no confident hit.

source: Goldbeck, Bernstein, Hillix, Marx (1957) Application of the half-split technique to problem-solving tasks, J Exp Psychol
finding: Earliest experimental test of the half-split technique found in search. Findings not seen. Citation volume is inconsistent between records.
numbers: Not available.
limits: Bibliographic record only. Not opened.
agent_relevance: Needed to answer whether people trained in half-split beat untrained people. Open next.
